title: First Julia scripts, values and observable output
outcome: Run a complete Julia script, trace bindings and distinguish a computed value from printed output.
key_terms: A `main.jl` file that Julia runs from top to bottom in a fresh process, so no state survives from an earlier run.
An association between a name and a value, so reassigning the name points it at a new value without changing the old one.
The result an expression returns, which a script shows only when the program prints it, unlike the REPL that echoes each result.
The concrete kind of a value, such as `Int64` or `String`, reported by `typeof` and attached to values rather than to names.
Julia compiles a method for the argument types of its first call, so that call can be slower than later calls.
approach: Treat each script as a fresh top-to-bottom evaluation. Read the source values, follow which name points at which value after every assignment, and only count something as output when `println` or `print` writes it. Timing questions are answered inside one process, because the classroom starts a new one for every Run.

exercises.title: Change a count
exercises.hint: Change one input and recompute the arithmetic.
exercises.answer: The output follows the current source values. A previous Run does not supply hidden counts.
exercises.why: Twenty accepted plus three rejected is 23, and the script recomputes that sum from the literals currently in the file each time it runs.
exercises.wrong: Editing the numbers but trusting the transcript from the previous Run reports the old total, because nothing from that earlier process is carried into the new one.
exercises.verify: Change the two literals, press Run, and confirm the printed total equals the new sum; `@test 20 + 3 == 23` states it as an assertion.

exercises.title: Keep a scalar snapshot
exercises.answer: Integers are immutable values; rebinding x does not rewrite the earlier value associated with y.
exercises.why: `y = x` makes `y` name the value 4. Assigning 10 to `x` afterward moves only the name `x`, so `y` still names 4.
exercises.wrong: Picturing `y` as a live link to the variable `x` predicts that `y` becomes 10, which treats names as storage cells rather than labels on values.
exercises.verify: Print both names after the rebinding and expect `x = 10` and `y = 4`; adding `@test y == 4` makes the snapshot permanent.

exercises.title: Print deliberately
exercises.task: Compare a bare arithmetic expression with println in a script.
exercises.expected: Only explicit output is guaranteed to appear in the script transcript.
exercises.answer: The REPL has display behavior that is not equivalent to running a source file.
exercises.why: A bare `2 + 3` line inside `main.jl` is evaluated and then discarded, since script mode has no automatic display; `println(2 + 3)` writes 5.
exercises.wrong: Copying a REPL session into a file and expecting each result to echo leaves an empty transcript and a wrong belief that the line failed.
exercises.verify: Run a file containing only `2 + 3`, then one containing `println(2 + 3)`, and compare the two transcripts line by line.

exercises.title: Inspect a type
exercises.expected: They are the environment integer type and Float64.
exercises.answer: The type describes the value representation and available methods, not whether the value is scientifically meaningful.
exercises.why: The literal `2` has no decimal point, so it is the platform integer, `Int64` on the 64-bit classroom runtime; `2.5` is a `Float64` literal.
exercises.wrong: Assuming every number is a float, as in some other languages, leads to `typeof(2) == Float64`, which is false and hides integer overflow behavior.
exercises.verify: Print `typeof(2)` and `typeof(2.5)`; the reference asserts `typeof(2.5) == Float64` among its exercise checks.

exercises.title: Diagnose a name
exercises.task: Misspell a variable in an owned copy of the program.
exercises.expected: An undefined-variable error identifies the failed name and source location.
exercises.hint: Inspect the first relevant submitted line.
exercises.answer: The diagnostic is evidence about a missing binding, not a reason to reinstall the runtime.
exercises.why: Misspelling `accepted` as `acepted` leaves a name with no binding, so Julia raises `UndefVarError` and points at the line that used it.
exercises.wrong: Reinstalling packages or restarting the runtime after this error treats a typo as an environment fault; the message already names the unbound identifier.
exercises.verify: Introduce the typo in an owned copy, read the first stack frame for the file and line, fix the spelling and confirm the run passes.

exercises.title: Explain first-call timing
exercises.task: Time a first and repeated call in one process.
exercises.expected: Their costs can include different amounts of compilation.
exercises.hint: The classroom starts a new process for each Run.
exercises.answer: Report the timing protocol; a cold call is not interchangeable with steady-state performance.
exercises.why: The first call compiles a method for its argument types, so `@time f(1)` on first use includes compilation that the second call in the same process skips.
exercises.wrong: Timing one call per Run and comparing it with a repeated call elsewhere mixes cold and warm measurements, since every classroom Run starts cold.
exercises.verify: Call `@time f(1)` twice inside one script and compare the reported allocations and time; report which call each number came from.
